issue: #633 (R5 item 9) — the step-0 ExUnits precondition decision 0005 amendment A3 attaches to giving `ledger_output_v1.parse_script_ref`'s tag-0 arm a structural predicate. Rows pinned here because the precondition FAILED and an owner-ruled wave item was dropped on the strength of them.
spec: docs/midgard/decisions/0005-owner-rulings-2026-08-18.md §A3 (the ruling and its precondition), with docs/spec/midgard-tx.md §5.5 for the reference-script field and §6.2 for output canonicity; GOAL_SPEC §3.3 for the basis. The spec re-point for the dropped item is tracked on #633 and is not this lane's.
note:
Decision 0005 amendment A3 gates wave item 9 -- giving `ledger_output_v1.parse_script_ref`'s tag-0 arm a canonical native-script structural predicate -- on an R3-style ExUnits measurement of the `accepted_transaction_v1` arm's worst case, taken BEFORE any on-chain commitment. These rows are that measurement. It FAILED, the item dropped out of the #617 wave, and this ledger is what makes the failure re-checkable when the follow-up ruling is written.

**The verdict, at the frozen basis.** `GOAL_SPEC_EXECUTION_BASIS_V1` is 13,200,000 memory units / 8,000,000,000 cpu units (`scripts/exec-ledger-within-basis-v1.mjs`; GOAL_SPEC §3.3 retires the 11,200,000 figure earlier benches derived from the stale Conway cap, and the lane's first commit message quoted the retired figure -- history is immutable, this file is the correction). Against it, `worst_case_deep_predicate` -- the largest payload the arm can ever see, 16,341 bytes and 5,447 nodes -- measures 1,076,971,016 mem / 360,206,747,738 cpu: **81x over on memory**, 45x on cpu, with nothing else in the transaction. The basis is exhausted at **67 nodes** on the deep shape and **76** on the wide one. The 16,384-node bound the scan carries is a STAGED-machine bound precisely because one L1 transaction cannot carry that scan.

**No cheaper faithful driver rescues it, and that is measured rather than argued.** `native_script_v1.inspect_native_script` -- the ready, total, re-encode-compare predicate A3 names as the alternative -- exhausts the same basis at about **100** nodes. A bare `cbor.deserialise` of the payload, which does no scanning at all and is therefore a floor under any one-shot driver anyone could write, exhausts it at about **250**. Two orders of magnitude short of 16,384 in every direction. Refuting this verdict needs a driver cheaper than reading the bytes.

**What the rows are.** Eight curve points, four per shape, at 65 / 257 / 1,025 / 4,097 nodes; a builder-only baseline for each worst-case vector, so the predicate's marginal cost is a difference rather than a whole-test reading (both baselines are around 83-89 K mem, under 0.01% of either worst case, which is what the doubling-concatenation builder buys); five comparison-arm readings on the two independent drivers; and the two reachable worst cases, each in its own module. Every vector is built programmatically by `midgard/native_script_payload_vectors_v1`.

**The derivations, and their cross-check.** The four node counts published above are two-point linear extrapolations recomputed by the verifier from the fresh readings, in exact integer arithmetic, never restated. They are not a fit anyone has to take on faith: extrapolating the deep 65-node and 4,097-node rows out to 5,447 nodes predicts 1,076,978,099 mem against a measured 1,076,971,016 -- 0.0007% high -- and the wide pair predicts 949,479,396 against a measured 949,469,452. Cost is linear in node count over an 84-fold range, at about 197,726 mem/node deep and 174,338 wide, so the crossing points are readings rather than guesses.

**A reachability correction the ruling does not carry.** A3 quotes the §5.4 per-field bound of 32,768 bytes. That bound is NOT reachable here: `parse_script_ref` is private to `ledger_output_v1`, and every route to it passes `max_output_canonical_cbor_bytes` (16,384) first. Subtracting the 43-byte minimum output envelope (`native_script_payload_vectors_v1.tag0_payload_envelope_bytes` derives it part by part) gives 16,341 bytes as the largest tag-0 payload the arm can ever see, and that is what the worst cases are built to. The unreachable 32,768-byte case was attempted and is past the tooling frontier -- `deep_payload(32768)`, 10,922 nodes, aborts the evaluator with "memory allocation failed" under a 16 GiB address-space cap -- which is recorded here rather than run, because the verdict does not need it: the REACHABLE case is already 81x over.

**The reach set, if it were wired anyway.** Measured by wiring the predicate into the tag-0 arm, building a scratch blueprint and diffing against c98cd0bf, then reverting: three validators move out of 444, not the two A3 predicts -- `fraud_proofs/transition_trace/accepted_transaction_v1`, `fraud_proofs/transition_trace/deposit_v1`, and `fraud_proofs/validation_trace/cek_context_step_semantic_v1`. The third is not named in the ruling and reaches the arm through `validation_machine_v1` -> `script_context_v1.tx_out_data_v1` -> `decode_canonical_output`; unlike `deposit_v1`, whose projected output is built with `script_ref: None` (`transition-trace/proof.ak:901`), that is a live runtime reach. It makes the budget verdict strictly worse. The branch as committed leaves `parse_script_ref` untouched and moves ZERO of the 444 validator hashes.

**What these rows do NOT claim.** (1) That the predicate is wrong. It is a faithful one-shot of the staged machine's own scan -- same `token_at_v1`, same `frame_for_token_v1` / `apply_child_v1`, same bounds, same exact-consumption finalize -- and it is correct and tested (`native-script-scan-v1.test.ak`, the `one_shot_*` refusals). What fails is the budget, not the logic. (2) That a STAGED tag-0 predicate is infeasible. `ledger_output_proof_v1` already scans native scripts across many transactions; this ledger prices the ONE-SHOT arm, which is the only thing A3's item 9 asked for. (3) That the vectors are valid L2 transactions. They are the worst shapes the ARM admits, which is what bounds its cost. (4) That the builder-only baselines are subtracted by the gate: the verifier judges absolute rows and recomputes the node-count derivations; the ~83 K subtraction is arithmetic a reader does over rows this file pins.

**Running this ledger, and a memory constraint that is part of the evidence.** The deep worst case peaks around 12.6 GB of host memory (38 s), the wide one around 0.6 GB (7 s). Aiken evaluates a module's selected tests in PARALLEL, so the two worst cases in ONE `aiken check` invocation exhaust a 16 GiB address space -- which is why they live in separate modules, and why `run-focused-check.mjs`, which puts every selector it is handed into one invocation, is called once per module here. For the same reason a full `aiken check` over the whole tree, which evaluates all three modules in one process, needs `RAYON_NUM_THREADS=1` to stay under 16 GiB; it passes there at a 12.5 GB peak. That is a property of the evaluator's parallelism and not of any single test: no test in this tree needs more than 12.6 GB on its own.

Regenerate with `MIDGARD_AIKEN_BIN=<fork> node scripts/verify-native-script-scan-exec-ledger-v1.mjs --update`, and move any reported number in the same commit. `--update` rewrites the raw mem/cpu rows and the recomputed derived integers; it does NOT rewrite `nodes`, `basisFit`, `infeasibility`, `ruling` or any `claim`, and it is not a bypass -- a row or selector that did not run, an `exceeds` row with no declared exception, or a fresh reading that contradicts a recorded `basisFit` fails in update mode too and the ledger is not rewritten. An `exceeds` row that starts fitting is the failure this ledger most wants to catch: it would mean wave item 9 is back. Provisional on the same footing as every other ledger in this directory; formal closure is Phase 7's, against the Phase-6 blueprint.

modules.neutralisationNote: Two selectors, both mutation-verified rather than assumed. (1) `curve_vectors_carry_the_node_counts_the_ledger_divides_by` is the shape guard: every `nodes` value in this module's rows is the divisor the derivations use, so shrinking a vector to make a row cheaper goes red here before it can be re-pinned. (2) `harness_predicates_refuse_a_malformed_payload` is the discrimination guard: a predicate that returned `True` for anything would price the same and mean nothing. It also records the one honest asymmetry between the arms -- `cbor.deserialise` ACCEPTS the malformed native script, because `82 07 00` is perfectly good CBOR, which is exactly why it is a lower bound on driver cost rather than a rival predicate.

modules.neutralisationNote: The deep worst case is alone in its module so that this invocation evaluates it without the wide one; its guards are what make the row a reading of the shape the note describes. `worst_case_deep_vector_is_the_reachable_maximum` pins 16,341 bytes / 5,447 nodes / stack depth 5,446 and that no further node fits; `worst_case_deep_shape_opens_one_frame_per_container` pins that the depth quoted is the SCAN's `stack_depth` and not the tree's height, on a two-container analogue; `worst_case_deep_predicate_refuses_a_malformed_payload` is the discrimination guard. The byte cap is derived from `ledger_output_v1.max_output_canonical_cbor_bytes`, so moving the whole-output cap reddens the first guard rather than silently re-pinning a smaller worst case.

worst_case_deep_predicate.infeasibility: THE READING THE VERDICT RESTS ON. The largest tag-0 payload `ledger_output_v1.decode_canonical_output` can ever admit -- 16,341 bytes, 5,447 nodes -- costs 81.6x the memory basis and 45.0x the cpu basis with nothing else in the transaction. Wiring the predicate into `parse_script_ref`'s tag-0 arm would make `accepted_transaction_v1`, `deposit_v1` and `cek_context_step_semantic_v1` unspendable against a payload an operator chooses freely.
